Massive suspicious bulk orders for used books have led many booksellers to believe these books are actually being purchased on behalf of AI companies, which then scan the book contents and use them as training material—all without the authors' consent or any payment.

An AirTag tucked inside a batch of rare books and shipped along with the order seems to confirm this theory, as the tracker ultimately ended up at an Amazon AI training facility…

Used booksellers typically only receive orders for a single title or a small number of related books. However, for quite some time now, many booksellers have reported receiving bulk orders for used books that seem to have nothing in common.

They suspect these books are being bought by AI companies, which then remove the spines and use high-speed scanners to digitise the text so that AI systems can use them as training material.

Doing this not only happens without their knowledge, but also without paying any royalties—at the very least it's unethical, but there has never been solid evidence to prove it's actually happening. An investigation by 404 Media seems to have shifted that picture.

The report itself is behind a paywall, but TNW relayed the findings, pointing out that the tracker used was indeed an AirTag, and that employees at the facility personally confirmed what was going on there.

Used books are particularly valuable because books published after 2022 are very likely to contain text written or edited by AI systems; in other words, they could well be using AI-generated content to train AI systems. While publishing contracts almost uniformly explicitly prohibit authors from using AI-generated content, there's a good chance some people ignore this rule. As for self-published books, there is effectively no oversight at all.

Part of the problem is that intellectual property law has yet to catch up with such practices. While doing this is likely already illegal in the UK, a 2025 ruling in the US shockingly found this behaviour to be legal, deeming it a "transformative" use of copyrighted works.
